nodes.summary: For a valid key $(y, p, q)$ for the modulus $N$, every bit $b$ and every unit $x$ modulo $N$, trapdoor decryption with $p$ and $q$ of the encryption of $b$ under $y$ with randomness $x$ returns $b$.
nodes.title: Correctness of Goldwasser–Micali encryption of one bit

nodes.summary: Given the factors $p$ and $q$ and a residue $c$ modulo $N$, output $0$ if $c^{\lfloor p/2 \rfloor} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ and $c^{\lfloor q/2 \rfloor} \equiv 1 \pmod q$, and $1$ otherwise. Only two modular powers are computed, so the definition is executable.
nodes.title: Goldwasser–Micali trapdoor decryption of one bit

nodes.summary: In a commutative group, with a public element $y$ and randomness $x$, the bit $0$ is encrypted as $x^2$ and the bit $1$ as $y x^2$. The scheme uses the group of units modulo $N$.
nodes.title: Goldwasser–Micali encryption of one bit

nodes.summary: Changing the $j$-th randomness $x_j$ to $x$ in a bitwise encryption changes only the $j$-th ciphertext component, which becomes the encryption of $m_j$ with randomness $x$.
nodes.title: Encrypting with updated randomness

nodes.summary: An $\ell$-bit message $m$ is encrypted with randomness $x_1, \dots, x_\ell$ (units modulo $N$) componentwise: the $i$-th ciphertext component is the encryption of the bit $m_i$ with randomness $x_i$.
nodes.title: Bitwise Goldwasser–Micali encryption

nodes.summary: The coins of the hybrid reduction: the distinguisher's coins together with an independent uniform vector of $\ell$ units modulo $N$.
nodes.title: The coins of the hybrid reduction

nodes.summary: For $\ell$-bit messages $m$ and $m'$ and $0 \le j \le \ell$, the message whose bits before position $j$ are those of $m'$ and whose bits from position $j$ on are those of $m$. The $0$-th hybrid is $m$, the $\ell$-th is $m'$, and consecutive hybrids differ in at most one position.
nodes.title: The `j`-th hybrid message

nodes.summary: From a distinguisher $D$ for $\ell$-bit ciphertexts, a message $u$ and a position $j$: on the public key $y$, a residuosity challenge $z$ and coins $(r, x_1, \dots, x_\ell)$, encrypt $u$ bitwise with randomness $x$, replace the $j$-th component by $z$ (if $u_j = 0$) or by $y z$ (if $u_j = 1$), and run $D$ with coins $r$. One call to $D$ and $\ell$ encryptions of single bits.
nodes.title: The hybrid reduction at position `j`

nodes.summary: If each of the $\ell$ hybrid reductions built from a distinguisher $D$ has residuosity advantage at most $\varepsilon$, then $D$ has advantage at most $\ell \varepsilon$ between encryptions of the two $\ell$-bit messages.
nodes.title: Bitwise Goldwasser–Micali loses a factor `ℓ`

nodes.summary: For every distinguisher $D$ and all $\ell$-bit messages $m$, $m'$, the distinguishing advantage of $D$ between encryptions of $m$ and of $m'$ under the `ℓ`-bit scheme is at most where $B_j$ is the hybrid reduction at position $j$ built from $D$ and the $j$-th hybrid message, and $\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{QR}}$ is the residuosity advantage. For positions where $m$ and $m'$ agree, consecutive hybrid messages coincide…
nodes.title: The hybrid argument for bitwise Goldwasser–Micali encryption

nodes.summary: For every distinguisher, message $w$ and position $j$, the indistinguishability experiment of the `ℓ`-bit scheme on $w$ equals the experiment that draws a uniform randomness vector, then an independent uniform unit $x$, and gives the distinguisher the bitwise encryption of $w$ with its $j$-th component replaced by the encryption of $w_j$ with randomness $x$.
nodes.title: The `ℓ`-bit experiment with one coordinate resampled

nodes.summary: Let $u$ and $v$ be $\ell$-bit messages that differ exactly at position $j$. For every distinguisher $D$, the indistinguishability experiments of the `ℓ`-bit scheme on $u$ and on $v$ are the worlds $0$ and $1$ of the residuosity experiment for the hybrid reduction built from $D$, $u$ and $j$, with its coins. In world $1$ with $u_j = 1$ the component $y \cdot y x^2 = (y x)^2$ is an encryption of $0$ because $y x$ is…
nodes.title: One hybrid step

nodes.summary: For one-bit messages, the indistinguishability experiment of the Goldwasser–Micali scheme on the message $b$, for any distinguisher and coins, is the residuosity experiment in world $b$.
nodes.title: Distinguishing Goldwasser–Micali ciphertexts is deciding residuosity

nodes.summary: If every distinguisher (with the given coins) has advantage at most $\varepsilon$ in the residuosity experiment, then the one-bit Goldwasser–Micali scheme has indistinguishable encryptions with error $\varepsilon$, all one-bit messages being given the same length.
nodes.title: All-distinguisher form: residuosity against every distinguisher gives indistinguishable encryptions (vacuous against unbounded distinguishers)

nodes.summary: For an eavesdropper $A$, a public key $y$ and coins $r$, write $Q_b$ for the probability that the reduction outputs $1$ in world $b$ of the residuosity experiment, and $E_b$ for the probability that $A$ outputs $1$ on an encryption of its message $m_b$ (both over the uniform unit $x$ only). Then $Q_1 + E_0 = Q_0 + E_1$. When $m_0 = m_1$ both $Q_b$ vanish and $E_0 = E_1$; otherwise $Q_0 = E_0$ and $Q_1 = E_1$.
nodes.title: The reduction for one key and one coin

nodes.summary: A valid key for the modulus $N$ is a triple $(y, p, q)$ of a unit $y$ modulo $N$ that is not a square and of distinct primes $p, q$ with $pq = N$. Goldwasser and Micali also require $y$ to have Jacobi symbol $+1$, so that the public key does not reveal $y$ as a non-residue; correctness does not need it, and the condition is not part of this definition. The test module exhibits the key $(2, 3, 5)$ for $N = 15$,…
nodes.title: A valid Goldwasser–Micali key

nodes.summary: In a commutative group, the encryption $x^2$ of the bit $0$ is a square, for every $y$ and $x$.
nodes.title: Encryptions of `0` are squares

nodes.summary: In a commutative group, if $y$ is not a square then the encryption of a bit $b$ with any randomness $x$ is a square if and only if $b = 0$. This is why the owner of the factorization, who can test residuosity, can decrypt.
nodes.title: Residuosity reveals the bit

nodes.summary: Let $p \ne q$ be primes and let $c$ be a unit modulo $pq$. Then $c$ is a square modulo $pq$ if and only if $c^{\lfloor p/2 \rfloor} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ and $c^{\lfloor q/2 \rfloor} \equiv 1 \pmod q$. For odd $p$, $\lfloor p/2 \rfloor = (p - 1)/2$, which is the exponent of Euler's criterion; the statement also holds when one of the primes is $2$.
nodes.title: Goldwasser–Micali's Lemma 2

nodes.summary: In a product $R \times S$ of two types with multiplication, a pair $(a, b)$ is a square if and only if $a$ is a square in $R$ and $b$ is a square in $S$.
nodes.title: Squares in a product

nodes.summary: In a commutative monoid, a unit $c$ is the square of a unit if and only if $c$ is a square in the monoid: if $c = r^2$ then $r$ is itself a unit.
nodes.title: Square units

nodes.summary: For the key distribution concentrated on a key whose $y$ is not a square, the one-bit scheme does not have indistinguishable encryptions with error $\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon < 1$. This is an instance of the general unattainability of indistinguishability for correct public-key schemes.
nodes.title: The one-bit Goldwasser–Micali scheme is not indistinguishable against unbounded distinguishers

nodes.summary: In a commutative group, if $y$ is not a square then the encryption $y x^2$ of the bit $1$ is not a square for any $x$: from $y x^2 = r^2$ one would get $y = (r x^{-1})^2$.
nodes.title: Encryptions of `1` are non-squares

nodes.summary: For a key whose element $y$ is not a square, the distinguisher that tests whether its challenge is a square outputs $1$ on every $y x^2$ and never on $x^2$, so it has advantage $1$ in the residuosity experiment. Hence the hypothesis "every distinguisher has residuosity advantage at most $\varepsilon$" forces $\varepsilon \ge 1$: in this concrete model, where every function counts as a distinguisher, the theorems…
nodes.title: An unbounded distinguisher decides residuosity

nodes.summary: For every key distribution and every eavesdropper $A$, the eavesdropping ($\mathsf{PubK}^{\mathrm{eav}}$) advantage of $A$ against the one-bit Goldwasser–Micali scheme equals half the advantage, in the residuosity experiment, of the reduction built from $A$ with one call and the same coins. So an eavesdropper with guessing advantage $\varepsilon$ gives a distinguisher of $x^2$ from $y x^2$ with advantage…
nodes.title: Goldwasser–Micali's main theorem for one bit, per adversary

nodes.summary: If the reduction built from an eavesdropper $A$ has advantage at most $\varepsilon$ in the residuosity experiment, then the eavesdropping advantage of $A$ against the one-bit scheme is at most $\varepsilon / 2$.
nodes.title: Residuosity bounds transfer to Goldwasser–Micali, per adversary

nodes.summary: The quadratic-residuosity advantage of a distinguisher is the distinguishing advantage between the two worlds of the residuosity experiment: how much more often it outputs $1$ on $y x^2$ than on $x^2$, in absolute value.
nodes.title: Residuosity advantage

nodes.summary: For a fixed modulus $N$, a distribution of keys $(y, (p, q))$, a distribution of coins and a distinguisher $D$, the experiment in world $b$ draws a key, coins $r$ and a uniform unit $x$ modulo $N$, and outputs $D(y, z, r)$ where $z = x^2$ if $b = 0$ and $z = y x^2$ if $b = 1$. When $y$ is a non-residue with Jacobi symbol $+1$, the element $y x^2$ is a uniformly random non-residue with Jacobi symbol $+1$, so the…
nodes.title: The residuosity experiment

nodes.summary: From an eavesdropper $A$ against the one-bit scheme: on the public key $y$, a challenge $z$ and coins $r$, let $(m_0, m_1)$ be the two messages $A$ chooses. If $m_0 = m_1$, output $0$. Otherwise give $A$ the ciphertext $z$ if $m_0 = 0$ and $y z$ if $m_0 = 1$, and output its guess. A square $z = x^2$ is then an encryption of $m_0$, and $z = y x^2$ an encryption of $m_1$ (for $m_0 = 1$ because…
nodes.title: The reduction from Goldwasser–Micali to the residuosity experiment

nodes.summary: If every key in the support of the key distribution is valid, then the Goldwasser–Micali scheme is correct: every ciphertext of a bit decrypts to that bit.
nodes.title: Correctness of the Goldwasser–Micali scheme

nodes.summary: If every key in the support of the key distribution is valid, the `ℓ`-bit scheme is correct.
nodes.title: Correctness of bitwise Goldwasser–Micali encryption

nodes.summary: For a fixed modulus $N$ and a distribution of keys $(y, (p, q))$, the public-key scheme whose messages are $\ell$-bit strings: encryption draws independent uniform units $x_1, \dots, x_\ell$ and outputs the bitwise encryption; decryption applies trapdoor decryption to each component.
nodes.title: The Goldwasser–Micali scheme for `ℓ`-bit messages

nodes.summary: For a fixed modulus $N$ and a distribution of keys $(y, (p, q))$, the public-key encryption scheme whose messages are bits: key generation samples a key from the distribution, the public key is $y$ and the secret key is $(p, q)$; encryption of $b$ samples a uniform unit $x$ modulo $N$ and outputs the encryption of $b$ with randomness $x$; decryption is trapdoor decryption.
nodes.title: The Goldwasser–Micali scheme for one-bit messages

nodes.summary: Under the hypothesis of the all-distinguisher form for indistinguishability, the one-bit Goldwasser–Micali scheme is semantically secure with error $\varepsilon$, for any types of a priori information and of guesses.
nodes.title: All-distinguisher form: residuosity against every distinguisher gives semantic security (vacuous against unbounded distinguishers)

nodes.summary: Drawing a uniform vector in $U^\ell$ (for a finite nonempty set $U$, here the units modulo $N$) and then replacing its $j$-th coordinate by an independent uniform element of $U$ gives a uniform vector in $U^\ell$. The map $(v, x) \mapsto (v[j \mapsto x], v_j)$ is a bijection of $U^\ell \times U$, and the first marginal of the uniform distribution on a product is uniform.
nodes.title: Resampling one coordinate of a uniform vector

nodes.summary: For every adversary $A$ against the one-bit Goldwasser–Micali scheme, every distribution $X$ of the plaintext bit, every a priori information function $h$ and every target function $f$, the probability that $A$ wins the real semantic-security experiment is at most the probability that Goldreich's simulator (which runs $A$ on an encryption of $0$) wins the ideal experiment, plus the residuosity advantage of the…
nodes.title: Semantic security of Goldwasser–Micali for one bit, per adversary

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
